Case Study 14
Race Condition in XV6 Shared Data
Operating Systems | Department of CSE
L Nithish Kumar Goud    |    160124733327
Chaitanya Bharathi Institute of Technology | Faculty / semester / year: __________
1. Problem Statement
Multiple CPUs in XV6 share kernel data structures like the physical memory free list.
Without synchronization, concurrent access causes race conditions.
Two CPUs can read the same free-list head and return the same page to different processes.
This leads to duplicate page ownership — corrupting memory.
Goal: Demonstrate the inconsistency, then fix it using XV6's spinlock.
2. Introduction — Objectives
Understand race conditions and critical sections in kernel code.
Identify shared kernel data structures (kmem.freelist) in XV6.
Study why mutual exclusion is required for multi-CPU access.
Demonstrate data inconsistency when the lock is absent.
Show how XV6's spinlock prevents inconsistent results.
Based on Case Study 14: Race Condition in XV6 Shared Data.
2. Introduction — Motivation
Modern CPUs have multiple cores — kernel code runs in true parallelism.
A single corrupted page allocation can crash the entire OS.
Understanding synchronization is essential for OS and systems programming.
XV6 is a small, real OS — ideal for studying these mechanisms.
XV6 runs on QEMU with configurable CPU count, making it perfect for multi-core experiments.
3. Existing System — Background
XV6 manages free physical memory as a linked list (kmem.freelist).
kalloc() pops the head page; kfree() pushes a freed page back.
A spinlock (kmem.lock) protects all accesses to the free list.
Table 1. Shared kernel structures and their locks

Structure	Lock	Purpose
kmem.freelist	kmem.lock	Physical page free list
ptable.proc[]	ptable.lock	Process table
bcache	bcache.lock	Buffer cache for disk blocks
Source: MIT xv6 RISC-V kernel source code.
3. Existing System — Drawbacks
Single global lock → CPUs spin-wait under high contention.
If the lock is removed, no mechanism prevents concurrent modification.
The production allocator cannot be safely tested without risking kernel crash.
No built-in diagnostic to detect or report race conditions.
These drawbacks motivate a safe, isolated test module for experimentation.
4. Proposed Solution
Test-only kernel module mirrors the free-list pattern on two QEMU CPUs (harts).

XV6 production allocator
kept intact and safe

racecheck.c
Miniature list: P0 → P1 → P2

CASE 1 · UNLOCKED
Both CPUs pop without a lock
Inconsistent ownership

CASE 2 · SPINLOCK
acquire()/release() protect the pop
Consistent ownership
Audit function verifies the page ownership invariant after each case
The test module leaves XV6’s production allocator unchanged.
5. Working Flow — Overview

USER PROGRAM
racetest.c starts the experiment

INITIALIZE
raceinit() resets the test list

FORK
fork() × 2 creates two children

WORKERS
Each child enters kernel and pops from the list

WAIT
wait() × 2 waits for both children

CASE 1 · UNLOCKED
Run without the lock
Both cases run automatically when the user types “racetest” at the xv6 shell.

REPORT
racereport() audits and prints results

RESET LIST
Start the second case with a fresh list

CASE 2 · SPINLOCK
Repeat with acquire()/release()
5. Working Flow — The Critical Section
The kalloc() function performs a two-step operation on shared data:

acquire(&kmem.lock);           // Step 1: Acquire the lock
r = kmem.freelist;             // Step 2: Read the head pointer
if (r)
    kmem.freelist = r->next;   // Step 3: Advance the head
release(&kmem.lock);           // Step 4: Release the lock

1 · ACQUIRE
acquire(&kmem.lock)
Step 2 (read) and Step 3 (update) depend on each other.
If another CPU changes the head between those steps, Step 3 uses a stale value and the assumption breaks.
Source: kernel/kalloc.c — XV6 production allocator.

2 · READ
r = kmem.freelist

3 · UPDATE
kmem.freelist = r->next

4 · RELEASE
release(&kmem.lock)
6. Implementation — Shared Data Structure
Test module mirrors the production allocator pattern:
Initial state:  freelist → P0 → P1 → P2 → NULL
Source: kernel/racecheck.c — test-only module, safe to break.
6. Implementation — Unlocked Path (Race Condition)
Both CPUs execute this simultaneously — NO lock protection:
Both read P0 before either updates → both return P0 (duplicate!)
Source: kernel/racecheck.c lines 115–124. The rendezvous forces the interleaving.
6. Implementation — Unlocked Timeline
Table 2. CPU interleaving without lock (race condition)

Step	CPU 0 (Worker 0)	CPU 1 (Worker 1)
T1	READ head → gets P0	READ head → gets P0
T2	SAVE next → P1	SAVE next → P1
T3	— rendezvous —	— rendezvous —
T4	WRITE head = P1	WRITE head = P1
T5	RETURN P0  ✓	RETURN P0  ✗ DUPLICATE
Result: P0 given to BOTH processes. Head = P1. INCONSISTENT.
Figure 1. Timeline of unlocked free-list pop showing duplicate allocation.
6. Implementation — Spinlock Path (Fix)
XV6's acquire()/release() wraps the entire critical section:
First CPU gets P0, second waits → then gets P1. No duplicates.
Source: kernel/racecheck.c lines 126–133. Uses XV6's real spinlock.
6. Implementation — Spinlock Timeline
Table 3. CPU interleaving with spinlock (serialized access)

Step	CPU 0 (Worker 0)	CPU 1 (Worker 1)
T1	— rendezvous —	— rendezvous —
T2	acquire(lock) ✓ GOT IT	acquire(lock) SPINNING...
T3	READ head → gets P0	(waiting)
T4	WRITE head = P1	(waiting)
T5	release(lock)	acquire(lock) ✓ GOT IT
T6		READ head → gets P1
T7		WRITE head = P2
T8	RETURN P0  ✓	RETURN P1  ✓
Figure 2. Timeline showing how spinlock serializes the critical section.
6. Implementation — User Program (racetest.c)
Source: user/racetest.c. System calls wired in kernel/syscall.c.
6. Implementation — Build & Run

STEP 1 · OPEN WSL
Open Ubuntu
wsl -d Ubuntu-24.04
Requires: gcc-riscv64-linux-gnu and qemu-system-misc installed in WSL.

STEP 2 · NAVIGATE
cd "/mnt/c/Users/HP/Documents/OS record/OS CASE STUDY/case_study_14_rebuild/xv6-riscv"

STEP 3 · BUILD + BOOT
make clean
make -j4 DETFLAGS= qemu CPUS=2

STEP 4 · RUN TEST
At the xv6 shell, type:
racetest

STEP 5 · EXIT QEMU
Press Ctrl+A, release, then press X
6. Implementation — Demo Output

[xv6 race demo] UNLOCKED free-list pop
  user workers ran on harts 0 and 1
  head values read: P0 and P0
  allocated pages: P0 and P0
  same page returned twice: YES
  free-list head after both pops: P1
  page IDs appearing exactly once: 2 / 3
  invariant: INCONSISTENT
  xv6 check: PASS

[xv6 race demo] SPINLOCK free-list pop
  user workers ran on harts 0 and 1
  allocated pages: P0 and P1
  same page returned twice: NO
  free-list head after both pops: P2
  page IDs appearing exactly once: 3 / 3
  invariant: CONSISTENT
  xv6 check: PASS

XV6 RACE DEMO: PASS (inconsistency reproduced; spinlock fixed it)
Figure 3. Captured XV6 terminal output showing both test cases.
7. Results
Table 4. Comparison of results — Unlocked vs. Spinlock

Criteria	Without Lock	With Spinlock
CPU 0 gets	P0	P0
CPU 1 gets	P0 (duplicate!)	P1 (unique)
Free list after	P1 → P2	P2
Duplicate allocation	YES	NO
Pages counted once	2 / 3	3 / 3
Data integrity	INCONSISTENT	CONSISTENT
Real-world impact	Memory corruption	Safe allocation
Source: XV6 kernel audit function in racecheck.c.
8. Conclusion — What We Learnt
A lock must cover the full read-and-update that preserves an invariant.
Without mutual exclusion, two CPUs return the same page — data corruption.
XV6's spinlock (acquire/release) serializes access to the critical section.
The same principle applies to any shared structure: process tables, buffers, caches.
Key learning: synchronization is not optional in multi-CPU kernels.
8. Conclusion — Future Scope & Applications
Test with more CPUs (4, 8) to study increased contention.
Implement per-CPU free lists to reduce lock contention.
Explore other primitives: mutex, semaphore, reader-writer locks.
Apply to real-world systems: database engines, web servers, RTOS.
Table 5. Synchronization in real-world applications

Application Domain	Shared Resource	Sync Method
Database Systems	Buffer pool / page cache	Latch / mutex
Web Servers	Connection pool	Semaphore
RTOS / Embedded	Shared I/O registers	Spinlock / disable IRQ
References: MIT xv6 RISC-V book (Locking chapter), github.com/mit-pdos/xv6-riscv
